sourceLine: your hydraulic hand and industrial results, and the questions line engineers ask before they deploy

cards.title: Cycle Time Is the Production Gate
cards.angle: Figure's BMW Spartanburg pilot ended November 2025 reporting 90,000 parts and a per-shift accuracy goal, with no cycle time published. A line engineer reads success rate and takt together or not at all.
cards.evidence: Your June 2026 result is 99.5 percent or better success at a 2.54 second cycle, validated against a Tier 1 supplier's live production benchmarks, on off-the-shelf arms rather than Phoenix. Your release states the two numbers; the article explains why the second one is the harder of the two.

cards.title: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real on a Hydraulic Hand
cards.angle: Teleop data costs $15 to $80 an hour in the West against roughly $3 in China, a labor arbitrage a Vancouver company cannot win. A policy trained entirely in simulation changes the cost of a training hour to compute.
cards.evidence: Your April 2026 demo transferred a sim-only policy to a real hydraulic hand, reorienting a cube ten consecutive times without a drop, trained on thousands of parallel hands in Isaac Lab. Hydraulics are harder to simulate than electric actuators, which is why the result deserves a longer explanation than a release.

cards.title: What DoF Counts Do Not Tell You About Hands
cards.angle: Unitree's H2 Plus (June 2026) lists 22-DoF tactile hands at a $100,000 robot price, matching your 21-DoF hydraulic hand on paper. Matching counts say nothing about force density, disturbance rejection or surface wear at factory cycle counts.
cards.evidence: Your RL hand work reports in-hand reorientation under a 500 g load not seen in training, and the May 2026 Zeon partnership targets elastomers that balance toughness with tactile precision. The piece sets out the measurements a buyer should ask for instead of DoF, without claiming yours win on each.
